bull_thesis: Eastroc (Dongpeng) is one of the cleaner compounding franchises in Asian consumer staples, and the ~50% fall from its 2025 highs has taken a wide-moat business from a euphoric multiple down to a reasonable one. The core is Dongpeng Special Drink, the number-one energy drink in China by volume (roughly two of every five bottles), still growing about 20% and gaining share with RISING gross margin (44.8% in 2025 to 46.9% in the first quarter of 2026). The economics are excellent: net margin ~21%, free-cash-flow margin ~19%, return on equity near 40%, return on invested capital ~23%, a deeply negative working-capital cycle (customers effectively pre-fund the business), and after the February 2026 Hong Kong listing a net-cash fortress of roughly 15.9 billion yuan — about a sixth of the H-share's market value sitting in cash. Strip that cash out and the H-share trades near 13x forward earnings for a franchise compounding ~20% with 40% returns on equity, which is inexpensive. The market is also discounting to near zero two real options: the HK$10 billion of fresh capital aimed at South-East Asia (an Indonesia joint venture with the Salim group, teams in Vietnam and Malaysia), and continued Southbound Stock Connect buying (mainland investors have been able to buy the H-share since March 2026), which supports a tighter-than-usual discount to the mainland A-share. Conditions the bull case needs: the second growth curve (the Shui Bu La electrolyte drink) must restabilise rather than collapse, the core energy franchise must keep compounding, and the early-August cornerstone lock-up supply must be absorbed. If those hold, the stock re-rates back toward the low end of its historical range as earnings compound.
bear_thesis: This is a quality-re-rating story dressed up by the screener as deep value, and at today's price the margin of safety is thin while a dated supply shock sits right ahead. The premium that carried the stock to its 2025 highs was built on the second growth curve, and that engine is visibly stalling: the Shui Bu La electrolyte line grew +280% in 2024, +119% in 2025, and only +13.2% in the first quarter of 2026 as Nongfu Spring, Mengniu, Master Kong and Evergrande Bingquan flooded the category. So the market is not mispricing terminal decline; it is correctly normalising a business that is maturing faster than the bulls admit, in a single country (China) whose consumer demand is soft, with a real if unquantified sugar-tax policy tail hanging over a sugar-based portfolio. The technical setup is worse than the fundamentals: only ~24% of shares float freely, the rest held in controlling-family and cornerstone blocks, and the cornerstone lock-up from the 3 February 2026 listing releases around early August 2026 into that thin float — a mechanical selling event, still pending as of this update. New H-share holders who bought near the top are underwater. And the H-share trades at only a ~20% discount to its own A-share, tight versus the 30-40% typical of dual-listed Chinese names, so the H can fall on a discount-widening even if the A holds. What confirms the bear: an August flush that breaks the 100.1 HKD low, a Q2/H1 print showing the electrolyte and total-revenue deceleration continuing, or any concrete sugar-tax proposal.
consensus_delta: The street is not pricing terminal decline here, so the usual deep-value question (is the market pricing death into a stable earner) is the wrong lens. Where we disagree with the market runs both ways. Against the bears who have driven the ~50% de-rating: they are extrapolating the Shui Bu La electrolyte stall (+13% in the first quarter of 2026, down from +119%) onto the whole company, when the core energy franchise is still a ~20% compounder gaining share with rising gross margin, and the ~16x forward multiple (~13x stripping out the ~16% of market value held as net cash) under-rates that durability and the 40% returns on equity. Against the bulls who treat the drop as a gift: at only ~16% upside to our base fair value, with a decelerating second engine, a soft China consumer, and only ~24% of the shares in free float, the asymmetry is not yet compelling. The specific street assumption we think is most fragile is the one embedded in the tight ~20% A-to-H discount — that Southbound demand will keep the H-share pinned near its A-share through the August lock-up; a forced-selling window can widen that discount first.
forcing_function: There is no positive, hard-dated re-rating catalyst. The one dated near-term event is adverse: the cornerstone lock-up expiry around early August 2026, which has not yet occurred as of this update. The genuine re-rating drivers are soft and on their own clock: evidence that the electrolyte and second-curve growth restabilises; tangible South-East Asia revenue from the HK$10 billion raised in February; and potential index inclusions (Hang Seng family membership or a heavier Southbound weight) that would broaden the buyer base. The right sequence is to let the August supply event clear the overhang, then let continued earnings delivery force the re-rating.
valley_of_death: The next three to nine months carry a real, dated supply risk rather than any solvency risk (the balance sheet is a fortress with ~15.9 billion yuan net cash, ~19% free-cash-flow margins, and a negative cash-conversion cycle). First and most concrete: the cornerstone and insider lock-up from the 3 February 2026 Hong Kong listing releases around early August 2026 into a free float of only ~24% — a mechanical wave of supply into a thin market, still pending as of this 2026-07-13 update. Second: continued electrolyte deceleration plus soft China consumer demand could produce a second-quarter or first-half 2026 print that, while still growing, disappoints the residual growth bulls and re-opens the de-rating (no such print has been released yet). Third: the H-share's ~20% discount to its A-share is tight for a dual-listed Chinese name, so the H can fall on a discount-widening even if the A-share holds. This is a positioning-and-supply valley, not a cash-burn or maturity-wall valley.
positioning_washout: Yes, and mechanically. Only ~24% of the shares float freely; the balance sits in controlling-family and cornerstone-investor blocks. The early-August 2026 cornerstone lock-up expiry is the first dated release into that thin float, and controlling-holder reduction plans on the mainland A-share have periodically pressured the stock in the past. New H-share holders who bought near the top are underwater and may capitulate. Under the current regime, which favours buying into mechanical forced-selling rather than ahead of it, this washout is the opportunity to exploit, not a reason to own the stock today.
moderator_conclusion: Wait for the wash-out. Eastroc (Dongpeng) is a genuinely high-quality, wide-moat compounder that the screener has mis-tagged as deep value on a corrupted, dual-listing, wrong-share-count reading (the real business is ~19x enterprise value to free cash flow and ~13x EV to EBITDA, not the 128x the screen shows, and the '-4% latest-quarter earnings per share' is a share-count dilution optic sitting on top of +28% net-profit growth). The franchise is compounding, margins are rising, returns on equity are ~40%, and there is a ~15.9 billion yuan net-cash fortress. But two things keep this off an aggressive-entry footing. First, the second growth curve that justified the premium — the Shui Bu La electrolyte line — is decelerating hard as Nongfu Spring, Mengniu and Master Kong flood the category, so the market is normalising a euphoric multiple, not mispricing decline; at ~16% upside to our 124 HKD base fair value against ~21% downside to an 85 HKD adverse case, the base-case risk/reward is roughly 0.75 to 1 against. Second, the setup is a positioning trap: only ~24% free float and a cornerstone lock-up releasing around early August 2026, with the H-share already trading at a tight ~20% discount to its own A-share that can widen in a forced-selling flush. The value case, judged on its own (a wide, widening moat, 40% returns, a net-cash cushion, ~13x forward ex-cash), is a notch better than the tradeable-today score — hence a higher value rating than conviction. The action: put this on the watch list and let the early-August forced-selling window do the work; a flush toward the mid-80s to mid-90s HKD, or clear evidence the second curve restabilises, is the entry, not 107 HKD ahead of the supply.

bull_thesis: Eastroc Beverage makes energy drinks in China. Its flagship, Dongpeng Special Drink, is sold in a large 500-millilitre bottle at a low price through several million small independent retailers, and over five years it has taken the leading volume position in the category. The bull case is that the market has cut the price of a genuinely good business in half for reasons that are mostly about the pace of growth rather than the quality of the earnings. Start with what the shares actually cost. At HK$114.60 on 18 August 2026, and using roughly 727 million shares across both listings, the whole company is valued at about HK$83bn, or RMB 71.5bn at this week's exchange rate of 1.165 Hong Kong dollars per renminbi. Against that sits RMB 4.90bn of profit over the last twelve months, RMB 4.86bn of free cash flow (the cash left after running and expanding the business), and RMB 17.15bn of net cash - RMB 23.21bn of cash and short-term investments against RMB 6.06bn of total debt including leases. Net cash alone is about 24% of the market value. Strip it out and the operating business is being bought at roughly 9.3 times enterprise value to earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, and at about 12 times its after-tax profit. The free cash flow yield on the market value is about 6.8%. Today's market regime note says free cash flow, not revenue, is now the discriminator between winners and losers; on that test this name screens near the top. The earnings are unusually clean. Operating cash flow runs at 1.49 times reported profit. Accounts receivable are RMB 133m against a June-quarter revenue of RMB 6.53bn - under two days of sales, because distributors pay before they take delivery. The cash conversion cycle is negative 20.6 days, so suppliers and customers finance the working capital. There is no goodwill anywhere on the balance sheet. When a fast-growing consumer company slows, the tell is a receivables or inventory build; there is none here. Nothing about these numbers looks stretched. The business itself has not stopped working. First-half 2026 revenue of RMB 12.42bn was up 15.6% and first-half profit of RMB 2.86bn was up 20.4% - profit growing faster than sales, with net margin up 90 basis points to 23.0%. Gross margin has stepped up from a five-year band of 42 to 45 per cent to 46.9% in the March quarter and 49.2% in the June quarter. A company losing pricing power does not expand gross margin by 350 basis points. Return on equity is 33.7% and return on capital employed 29.0%. And management is behaving like an owner: after selling H-shares in Hong Kong in the first quarter of 2026 (RMB 9.76bn of financing inflow, share count from 676m to 734m, an implied issue price near HK$197 by arithmetic), it created RMB 1.04bn of treasury stock in the June quarter - selling near the high and buying back a third lower. Finally, the comparison set. Nongfu Spring trades at 17.6 times enterprise value to operating earnings and about 25.7 times profit; Monster Beverage at 29.9 times and about 42.9 times. Eastroc at 9.3 times is a fraction of either, on faster growth than Nongfu and a better balance sheet than both. If revenue settles at low-to-mid teens growth, margins hold anywhere near current levels, and the multiple recovers even part-way toward the global peer group, the shares are worth meaningfully more than today. The specific conditions the bull case needs: second-half 2026 revenue growth of at least 10 to 12 per cent; gross margin holding above 46 per cent; the second product line in hydration drinks continuing to scale; and the RMB 9.8bn raised in Hong Kong being spent on capacity that earns a return rather than sitting idle.
bear_thesis: The bear case is not that this is a bad business - it is that the cheapness is being measured against peak profits, on estimates that are still wrong, in a sector where every name has fallen together. First, the growth has genuinely broken step. Revenue grew 31.8% in full-year 2025. It grew 21.5% in the March 2026 quarter. It grew 10.8% in the June 2026 quarter - RMB 6.53bn against RMB 5.89bn. That is the top line more than halving its pace inside six months, in what is seasonally the strongest part of the year for a summer drink. One soft peak quarter is a data point; the risk is that it is the run-rate. Second, and more important, the margins are at a five-year record with an identifiable cause that is reversing right now. Gross margin was 44.4%, 42.3%, 43.1%, 44.8% and 44.8% in the five years to 2025 - the company never escaped that band. It is now 49.2%. The bottles are made from polyethylene terephthalate, a plastic derived from oil, and sugar is the other main input; both were cheap through 2025 and early 2026. Today's regime note records Brent crude round-tripping from $79.36 on 4 August to about $91 after the US-Iran talks lapsed on 17 August. If roughly 350 basis points of that gross margin is input cost rather than pricing, reversion takes about RMB 850m off annualised gross profit and about RMB 640m off after-tax earnings - some 13% of the trailing figure. A multiple of 14.6 times peak earnings is not 14.6 times normal earnings. Third, the published estimates are stranded. Seventeen analysts carry a 2026 revenue figure of RMB 28.82bn, up 38%. The first half delivered RMB 12.42bn. Reaching the consensus would require a second half of RMB 16.41bn against RMB 10.13bn a year ago - up 62% - in a business whose second half is seasonally smaller than its first. Those numbers have to come down by roughly 17%, and the downgrade cycle has not visibly happened. A stock can be cheap on the right numbers and still fall while the wrong ones are being corrected. Fourth, the equity raise permanently reset the returns. Shareholders funds went from RMB 9.42bn in December 2025 to RMB 19.52bn in June 2026 while profit did not double. Return on equity was 35.8%; on the new base a RMB 5.5bn profit is closer to 26%. Return on invested capital has already fallen from 22.6% to 17.8%. The premium multiple this company used to command was a premium for a 35% return on equity that no longer exists. And the money was raised from a position of strength - the company already held RMB 13.8bn of cash and generated RMB 4.86bn of free cash flow a year - at what proved to be within a whisker of the all-time high. Fifth, the capital spending is aggressive into a decelerating demand curve. Capital expenditure over the trailing year was RMB 2.41bn - 10.7% of revenue and 8.5 times depreciation. Net property, plant and equipment has gone from RMB 3.78bn in June 2024 to RMB 7.91bn in June 2026. Building capacity at that rate when volumes are slowing is the standard route by which a high-return Chinese consumer business becomes an average one. Sixth, the discount is not specific to this company. Mixue Group has fallen from HK$499.60 to HK$223.40, Want Want from HK$5.97 to HK$3.30, Nongfu Spring from HK$56.25 to HK$42.16. The whole Chinese branded-beverage complex is being re-rated on the same unresolved driver - domestic consumer demand - and Mixue, the closest recent Hong Kong listing, actually trades cheaper at 8.3 times operating earnings than Eastroc at 9.3 times. There is no single-name edge in the gap. Seventh, a large part of the apparent upside is an exchange-rate-and-listing artefact rather than value. The Shanghai A-shares closed at RMB 122.57 on 18 August; the Hong Kong shares at HK$114.60, which is RMB 98.34. The Hong Kong line trades at a 19.8% discount to the mainland line for identical ownership. That gap is a structural consequence of capital controls and a different investor base, and it very rarely closes. What would confirm the bear case: a third-quarter revenue print below 10% growth; gross margin retreating below 47%; the 2026 consensus revenue figure being cut toward RMB 24bn; or distributor prepayments, already down from RMB 5.98bn in December to RMB 5.13bn in June, falling further.
consensus_delta: The signal type here is deep value, so the question is whether the market is pricing terminal decline into a company whose earnings power is stable or growing. It is not - and that is precisely the problem with the bull case. What the market is actually doing is repricing a growth rate, and it has not finished. The place where we disagree with the market is narrower and more specific than the headline discount suggests, and it points both ways. Where the published numbers are plainly wrong: seventeen analysts carry a 2026 revenue estimate of RMB 28.82bn, up 38% on 2025. The first half of 2026 delivered RMB 12.42bn. To reach the consensus, the second half would have to produce RMB 16.41bn against RMB 10.13bn a year earlier - growth of 62% - in a business whose second half is seasonally smaller than its first (RMB 10.74bn versus RMB 10.13bn in 2025). That is not a stretch, it is an arithmetic impossibility. Our own bottom-up estimate, rolling the first half forward with 12% second-half growth at a 23% net margin, lands 2026 revenue near RMB 23.8bn and profit near RMB 5.5bn - the very bottom of the published RMB 5.47bn to RMB 6.10bn range. Estimates have to fall roughly 17% on revenue. The share price has already halved, so the market clearly knows something the models do not, but the formal downgrade cycle has not visibly run, and stocks tend to trade badly while it does. Where we disagree with the bears: the earnings quality is not in question. Operating cash flow at 1.49 times reported profit, receivables under two days of sales, a negative cash conversion cycle of 20.6 days, no goodwill, and RMB 17.15bn of net cash equal to about 24% of the market value. This is not a company whose reported profits are an accounting artefact, and a fair number of Chinese consumer de-ratings are exactly that. Profit is also still growing faster than revenue - 20.4% against 15.6% in the first half - with net margin up 90 basis points. Where we think both sides are looking past the real issue: the multiple everyone is quoting is being computed on record margins. Gross margin has stepped from a five-year 42-to-45 per cent band to 49.2% in the June quarter. The likely cause is cheap oil-derived plastic and cheap sugar. Today's regime note records Brent crude round-tripping from $79.36 on 4 August to about $91 after the US-Iran talks lapsed on 17 August. If about 350 basis points of that margin is input cost, reversion costs roughly RMB 640m of after-tax profit - 13% of trailing earnings - and 14.6 times becomes closer to 17 times. The bulls are treating a peak margin as a base, and the bears are arguing about volumes when the margin is the bigger number. One further correction to how the discount is usually framed: the gap to Nongfu Spring at 17.6 times operating earnings is not company-specific edge. Every Chinese branded-beverage name has de-rated together on the same unresolved driver, and Mixue Group - the closest recent Hong Kong listing - is actually cheaper at 8.3 times. And 19.8 points of the apparent discount is simply the structural gap at which these Hong Kong shares trade to the same company's Shanghai shares, which does not close.
forcing_function: For a deep-value name the question is what event forces the market to re-rate, and the honest answer here is that no single one exists. There is no buyback authorisation of a size that would move the shares, no activist, no asset sale, no dividend initiation, no strategic process. What there is, in order of how much it would move the price: the third-quarter report, which mainland-listed issuers must publish by 31 October 2026. This is the one genuinely fixed date. It is a routine disclosure with no contractual payout attached, but it settles the single open question - whether the June quarter's 10.8% revenue growth was a stumble or the new rate - and it will show whether the 49.2% gross margin survived the oil move. A third-quarter print reaccelerating above 15% with margin intact would break the bear case decisively. Below 10% with margin retreating would confirm it. Second, the estimate reset. Once the seventeen analysts carrying an unreachable RMB 28.82bn revenue number cut toward RMB 24bn, the shares stop being measured against an impossible bar. That is a soft catalyst with no fixed date and no contractual payout, but it is the one that changes the arithmetic of how the name screens. Third, the buyback. RMB 1.04bn of treasury stock appeared for the first time in the June 2026 quarter. If the company expands the programme materially, it converts the net cash from a static balance-sheet item into a per-share driver, and it is the most credible route by which the RMB 17.15bn of cash starts working for shareholders rather than sitting alongside them. Fourth, and outside management's control, Chinese domestic consumer demand. This is a third-party driver with no date, and it is the same driver moving every name in the peer group, so it delivers no advantage specific to this company. Notably absent, and worth saying explicitly: nothing in this thesis depends on a rate cut or a central-bank rescue, and nothing depends on the artificial-intelligence capital-expenditure cycle. The resolution driver is Chinese consumer demand and Chinese input costs, which is genuinely independent of the dominant shared factors in the current tape. That independence is the most attractive structural feature of the name.
valley_of_death: The risky window is the next three to nine months, and there are four distinct things that can go wrong before the value case has a chance to converge. This is not a cash-burn or maturity story - the company holds RMB 23.21bn of cash and short-term investments against RMB 6.06bn of debt, generates RMB 4.86bn of free cash flow a year and could repay every borrowing tomorrow. The risks are to the earnings estimate and the multiple, not to solvency. First and most immediate, the estimate reset. Consensus 2026 revenue of RMB 28.82bn has to come down toward RMB 24bn. Downgrade cycles in Chinese consumer names tend to arrive in a cluster once one house moves, and the price action while that happens is usually poor regardless of how cheap the shares already look. Second, the third-quarter report, due by 31 October 2026. The third quarter is a peak season for an energy drink; the June quarter grew only 10.8%. A third-quarter print below 10% would confirm that the June quarter was the run-rate rather than a weather or distribution artefact, and would validate the bear case on volumes. Third, the input-cost turn. Brent crude went from $79.36 on 4 August to about $91 this week with the strait of Hormuz under naval blockade at 84 transits a week, and the polyethylene terephthalate used for the bottles is an oil derivative. The pass-through into Chinese resin prices runs on a lag of roughly one to two quarters, which places the margin hit squarely inside this window. Record gross margin plus rising oil is an unstable combination. Fourth, the capital programme. Capital spending is running at RMB 2.41bn a year, 8.5 times depreciation, and net fixed assets have doubled in two years. If volume growth stays at 10%, that capacity arrives into a market that does not need it, and depreciation starts eating the margin from below just as input costs eat it from above. A secondary risk worth naming: the shares listed in Hong Kong in the first quarter of 2026, so any cornerstone or pre-listing lock-up would be expiring around now. No lock-up date could be verified from any source, so this is flagged as a possibility rather than asserted, but the shape of the drawdown - HK$227.69 to HK$100.10 within months of listing - is consistent with supply meeting a thinning bid.
positioning_washout: The forced-selling dynamics here are about a listing cohort rather than a dividend cut or an index event. Three mechanisms are visible in the price record. First, the recent-listing unwind. The Hong Kong line listed in the first quarter of 2026 at an implied price near HK$197 by our arithmetic from the accounts, traded to HK$227.69, and now sits at HK$114.60 - a fall of about 50% from the high and roughly 42% below the implied issue price. Whoever bought the placement is deeply underwater, and holders of that kind are structurally motivated sellers into any rally. Second, the cohort effect. Every Chinese consumer name that listed or re-rated in Hong Kong in this window has been sold together: Mixue Group from HK$499.60 to HK$223.40, Want Want from HK$5.97 to HK$3.30, Nongfu Spring from HK$56.25 to HK$42.16, while Tingyi - the slow-growing defensive in the group - sits within a whisker of its high at HK$13.58. That is not a company-specific verdict, it is a factor unwind: money is leaving Chinese consumer growth and staying in Chinese consumer value. Anyone owning this name owns that factor. Third, the estimate reset itself creates mechanical selling. Quantitative and growth-screening mandates hold positions on forward growth and earnings-revision signals. A 17% cut to 2026 revenue estimates flips both signals negative and forces sales irrespective of price. There is a genuine offset. The company created RMB 1.04bn of treasury stock in the June 2026 quarter, having created none previously - it is buying its own shares back, at prices roughly a third below where it sold them. That is a real, funded bid from the one buyer with the best information. It is not large enough to absorb a determined factor unwind, but it does put a body under the market and it says something about how management sees the price. On balance, the washout is well advanced but not obviously complete: the price is only about 15% up off its fifty-two-week low of HK$100.10, and the estimate downgrades that would trigger the last leg of mechanical selling have not yet happened.
moderator_conclusion: The recommendation is to watch this one rather than buy it today, and the specific level to wait for is HK$95 to HK$100 - the fifty-two-week low area - or, alternatively, a third-quarter report on or before 31 October 2026 showing revenue growth back above 15% with gross margin holding above 47%. Either would do; today's price and today's information do not. Here is the reasoning. This is a good business at a fair price rather than a good business at a cheap price, and the difference matters. What is genuinely attractive: Eastroc holds the leading position in Chinese energy drinks with a brand and a distribution network into several million small retailers that is expensive and slow to replicate. The earnings are cash - operating cash flow at 1.49 times reported profit, receivables under two days of sales, a negative cash conversion cycle, no goodwill on the balance sheet. There is RMB 17.15bn of real net cash, about 24% of the market value at the Hong Kong price. Free cash flow of RMB 4.86bn is a 6.8% yield, and this week's regime note says free cash flow rather than revenue is the current discriminator, which favours the name. Profit is still growing faster than sales. Management sold shares near the high and is now buying them back. None of that is in dispute. What holds it back is arithmetic rather than sentiment. Our base-case fair value, built from the parts, is HK$131 - the operating business at 11 times operating earnings, deliberately between Nongfu Spring at 17.6 times and Mixue Group at 8.3 times, plus the net cash less the committed capital programme. That is about 14% above today's HK$114.60. Fourteen per cent is not a margin of safety; it is inside the error bars of the multiple we chose. And a sizeable part of even that 14% is not value at all - it is the 19.8% discount at which these Hong Kong shares trade to the same company's Shanghai shares at RMB 122.57, a structural gap driven by capital controls that very rarely closes. Strip that out and the base case is close to fully valued. Three further things argue for patience. First, the multiple is being paid on record margins. Gross margin has jumped from a five-year 42-to-45 per cent band to 49.2%, almost certainly on cheap oil-derived plastic and cheap sugar - and Brent went from $79.36 on 4 August to about $91 this week. That is roughly 13% of trailing earnings at risk on a lag of one to two quarters, which lands inside the window. Second, the published estimates are stranded 17% too high on 2026 revenue, and the downgrade cycle has not visibly run. Cheap stocks trade badly while their numbers are being cut. Third, the discount is not ours to claim: every Chinese branded-beverage name has fallen together on the same unresolved consumer-demand driver, and Mixue Group is actually cheaper. That is shared sector exposure, not single-name edge. On the catalyst, the honest position is that the two events that mattered - the Hong Kong listing and the first-half print - have both already happened, and neither helped the shareholder. What remains is a soft catalyst with no fixed date: an estimate reset and a consumer recovery. In this book a spent or undated catalyst is neither a plus nor a penalty, so the judgement rests entirely on the residual value case, and the residual value case is 14% of upside against 26% of downside to the adverse HK$85. That is the wrong way round. On the durability question, the moat is narrow but real and stable - the expanding gross margin is direct evidence a moat is not eroding, while the fall in return on invested capital from 22.6% to 17.8% is mostly the arithmetic consequence of doubling the equity base in the Hong Kong raise rather than competitive damage. There is no structural force threatening the terminal value of a company selling bottled caffeinated drinks in China; the risks are cyclical and competitive. This is not a value trap. It is simply not yet a bargain. Put it on the list, mark the level, and wait for either the price or the third-quarter numbers to come to us.

# Forensic dossier — Eastroc Beverage (Group) Co., Ltd. · 9980.HK (Hong Kong H-shares)

**Date of this review:** 18 August 2026
**Price used throughout:** HK$114.60 per H-share (Hong Kong Stock Exchange, ticker 9980), the live quote on 18 August 2026. The same company's mainland A-shares (Shanghai, ticker 605499) closed at RMB 122.57 the same day.
**Reporting currency:** the company reports in Chinese renminbi (RMB). Exchange rate used: 1 RMB = 1.165 Hong Kong dollars (derived from live dollar rates of 6.7306 renminbi and 7.8434 Hong Kong dollars per US dollar, 18 August 2026).

**An important caveat on sources.** No earnings-call transcript for this company could be obtained. The paid market-data service returns no transcripts, no news items and no analyst-rating history for either the Hong Kong or the Shanghai listing, and the general web-search budget for this session was exhausted before this name was reached. Chinese A-share issuers in the consumer-staples sector also do not typically hold English-language quarterly calls in the American style, so a transcript archive may simply not exist. Everything below is therefore built from the audited and interim financial statements, the live quotes, the published sell-side estimate consensus, and one independent price-and-ratio cross-check. Where a section would normally rest on management's spoken words, that is stated plainly rather than filled in. No quotation, guidance figure or management statement appears anywhere in this document, because none could be sourced.

---

## 1. Narrative arc

Eastroc makes energy drinks in China. Its flagship product, Dongpeng Special Drink, is sold in a 500-millilitre bottle at a low price point through a very large network of small independent retailers, and over the past five years it has taken the leading volume position in the Chinese energy-drink category. A second product line in electrolyte and hydration drinks, plus smaller lines in tea, coffee and juice, has been added on top.

Read through the financial statements alone, the story has three distinct chapters.

**Chapter one, 2021 to 2024 — a compounding machine.** Revenue went from RMB 6.98bn in 2021 to RMB 15.84bn in 2024, a compound annual rate of about 31%. Net profit went from RMB 1.19bn to RMB 3.33bn. Gross margin was flat-to-soft through this stretch (44.4% in 2021, dipping to 42.3% in 2022, back to 44.8% in 2024), so essentially all of the profit growth was volume and operating leverage, not price or mix. This is the profile of a brand winning shelf space.

**Chapter two, 2025 — the peak.** Revenue reached RMB 20.88bn, up 31.8%; net profit RMB 4.42bn, up 32.7%. Net margin hit 21.2%, then a record. The company also carried out a bonus share issue during the year, taking the share count from 520.0m to 676.0m — the weighted-average share count in the 2025 annual accounts is 676.0m against 520.0m in 2024, exactly 1.3 times, consistent with a three-for-ten capitalisation issue.

**Chapter three, 2026 — the raise, then the slowdown.** In the first quarter of 2026 the company listed H-shares in Hong Kong. The evidence is in the accounts: financing activities brought in RMB 9.76bn of cash in the March 2026 quarter, cash and equivalents jumped from RMB 5.68bn to RMB 14.90bn, shareholders' equity more than doubled from RMB 9.42bn to RMB 20.40bn, and the issued share count rose from 676.0m to 734.1m. The Hong Kong line's fifty-two-week high is HK$227.69 against today's HK$114.60. Taking RMB 9.76bn raised against roughly 58m new shares implies an issue price near RMB 169, or about HK$197 — which sits just under that fifty-two-week high and about 42% above where the shares trade today. That inferred issue price is an arithmetic reconstruction from the accounts, not a sourced fact, and should be treated as such; the direction of it, however, is unambiguous.

Then the growth broke step. Revenue in the June 2026 quarter was RMB 6.53bn against RMB 5.89bn a year earlier — up 10.8%. For the first half of 2026 as a whole, revenue of RMB 12.42bn against RMB 10.74bn is up 15.6%. Against a full-year 2025 growth rate of 31.8%, the top line has roughly halved its pace in six months.

The narrative arc, in one line: a company that compounded revenue at about a third a year for four years raised a large slug of equity in Hong Kong at what now looks like the top, and within two quarters printed its slowest growth in years. The shares have halved.

---

## 2. Claims versus financials (forensic)

With no transcript available, there are no management claims to test directly. What can be tested is the *published sell-side consensus* — which functions here as the market's version of management's story, since analyst models are built off company guidance and investor-relations contact. That test is the single most revealing thing in this file.

| What the consensus expects (17 revenue analysts, 8 EPS analysts) | What the accounts actually show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| 2026 revenue of RMB 28.82bn, up 38% on 2025 | First-half 2026 revenue of RMB 12.42bn, up 15.6% | **Cannot both be true.** To reach RMB 28.82bn, the second half would need RMB 16.41bn against RMB 10.13bn a year ago — up 62%. Eastroc's second half is seasonally *smaller* than its first (2025: RMB 10.74bn first half, RMB 10.13bn second). The consensus revenue number is stale and must come down. |
| 2026 net profit of RMB 5.84bn (range RMB 5.47bn to RMB 6.10bn) | First-half net profit RMB 2.86bn, up 20.4%; net margin 23.0% versus 22.1% | **Closer to reachable, at the low end.** Roll the first half forward with 12% second-half revenue growth and a 23% margin and the year lands near RMB 5.5bn — the bottom of the published range, not the middle. |
| 2026 earnings per share of RMB 8.64 | Trailing twelve-month earnings per share of RMB 6.74 (RMB 4.90bn over roughly 727m shares) | Requires 28% earnings growth in a year whose first half delivered 20% on 16% revenue growth. Reachable only if margins keep expanding. |
| 2027 revenue of RMB 33.68bn, 2028 of RMB 38.83bn | — | These build on the 2026 base. If 2026 lands near RMB 23.8bn rather than RMB 28.8bn, the whole forward curve resets roughly 17% lower. |

Three further forensic reads on the accounts themselves, all of which matter more than the headline growth rate:

**The margins are genuinely at a record, and that is a risk, not only a strength.** Gross margin by year: 44.4% (2021), 42.3% (2022), 43.1% (2023), 44.8% (2024), 44.8% (2025) — then 46.9% in the March 2026 quarter and 49.2% in the June 2026 quarter. That is roughly 400 basis points above a five-year band the company never previously escaped. The screener's own flag — margins running about 1.35 standard deviations above their historical peak — is corroborated by the raw numbers. The most likely driver is input costs: the bottles are polyethylene terephthalate, a plastic derived from oil, and sugar is the other main ingredient. Both were cheap through 2025 and early 2026. **Today's market regime note records Brent crude round-tripping from $79.36 on 4 August to about $91 after the Iran talks lapsed on 17 August.** If that holds, the exact tailwind producing the record gross margin reverses. Roughly 350 basis points of gross margin on annualised first-half revenue is about RMB 850m of gross profit, or around RMB 640m of after-tax profit — 13% of trailing earnings.

**The cash conversion is exceptionally clean, and there is no sign of channel stuffing.** Accounts receivable are RMB 133m against a June-quarter revenue of RMB 6.53bn — under two days of sales; the published days-sales-outstanding measure is 9.8 days. The cash conversion cycle is *negative* 20.6 days, meaning suppliers and customers finance the business. Operating cash flow runs at 1.49 times reported net profit. There is no goodwill on the balance sheet at all. When a company's growth slows, the first place a stretched story shows up is a receivables build or an inventory build; neither is present here. This is a strong green flag and it materially raises confidence that the reported profit is real cash profit.

**Returns on capital are falling, and the equity raise is the main reason.** Return on equity was 35.8% in the last full-year screen and is 33.7% on a trailing basis. Return on invested capital has fallen from 22.6% to 17.8%. But shareholders' equity went from RMB 9.42bn to RMB 19.52bn in two quarters while earnings did not move proportionally, so on the new equity base a RMB 5.5bn profit is a return on equity closer to 26%. This is arithmetic, not deterioration in the business — but it is a permanent reset of the number investors were paying a premium multiple for.

---

## 3. Tone and confidence trajectory

**Not assessable from primary evidence.** No transcripts, press releases or investor presentations for either listing could be retrieved. This section is deliberately left without a rating rather than inferred, because tone is exactly the sort of thing it would be easy and dishonest to invent.

Two behavioural signals stand in for tone, both drawn from actions rather than words:

- **The company raised roughly RMB 9.8bn of equity in Hong Kong in early 2026 when it did not obviously need it.** Before the raise it already held RMB 13.8bn of cash and short-term investments against RMB 7.06bn of debt, and it generated RMB 4.86bn of free cash flow over the trailing year. Raising a large slug of equity into strength, at what proved to be within a whisker of the all-time high, is skilful treasury management from the company's point of view. It is a poor outcome for whoever bought those shares. Read as a signal about management's own view of the valuation on offer, it is not encouraging.
- **The company began buying back stock in the June 2026 quarter.** Treasury stock of RMB 1.04bn appears on the June balance sheet where none existed in March. Buying back shares at HK$115 to HK$150 having sold them near HK$197 six months earlier is at least internally consistent with management believing the shares are now cheap.

---

## 4. Guidance credibility

**No company guidance could be sourced,** so guidance-versus-delivery cannot be tracked directly. Two indirect readings:

- The screener records a beat rate of six out of the last eight quarters (75%) against consensus estimates. That is a respectable, unremarkable record — consistent with a company that manages expectations competently but does not sandbag heavily.
- The far more troubling signal is the *gap that currently exists*. Seventeen analysts carry a 2026 revenue number that the first half has already made arithmetically unreachable. Either those models have not been updated since the interim results, or the company's investor-relations messaging has not reset expectations. In a market where the shares have already halved, the estimates being 17% too high is the unfinished business.

**Reliability rating: Medium, and provisional.** The financial statements are of high quality and internally consistent — that part is genuinely reassuring. But the credibility of the *forward narrative* is untested, because the forward narrative could not be obtained, and the one observable proxy for it (the street's numbers) is visibly wrong.

---

## 5. Analyst pressure points

Without call transcripts, the questions analysts actually pressed cannot be reported. The questions the *accounts* say they should be pressing are these, and each is a specific thing to watch for in the next disclosure:

1. **Is the June quarter's 10.8% growth the new run-rate, or a distribution or weather artefact?** Energy-drink volumes in China are heavily summer-weighted. One soft peak quarter is a data point; two is a trend.
2. **How much of the record 49.2% gross margin is input cost rather than pricing or mix?** With crude back near $91 this is now the most valuable single disclosure the company could make, and the one most likely to be answered vaguely.
3. **What is the RMB 9.76bn actually for?** Capital spending is running at RMB 2.41bn over the trailing year — 10.7% of revenue and *8.5 times* depreciation. Net property, plant and equipment has gone from RMB 3.78bn in June 2024 to RMB 7.91bn in June 2026. Building capacity at that pace into a decelerating demand curve is the classic way a high-return Chinese consumer business turns into a mediocre one.
4. **Why does the company carry RMB 5.67bn of short-term borrowings while holding RMB 23.21bn of cash and short-term investments?** This is a common and usually benign mainland treasury structure — borrow cheaply, park the proceeds in higher-yielding wealth-management products — but it does mean the headline net cash figure depends on those wealth-management products being genuinely liquid and unpledged.
5. **Distributor prepayments (contract liabilities) have fallen from RMB 5.98bn in December 2025 to RMB 5.13bn in June 2026** while revenue rose. That is money distributors have already handed over for goods not yet delivered, and it is one of the better forward-looking reads on channel enthusiasm in this business model. The comparison here is partly seasonal and the prior-year figure is not cleanly mapped in the available data, so this is flagged as a question, not a conclusion.

---

## 6. Red flags and green flags

**🔴 Red flags**

- **Growth halved in two quarters.** 31.8% for full-year 2025; 21.5% in the March 2026 quarter; 10.8% in the June 2026 quarter.
- **Margins at a five-year record with an identifiable, reversing cause.** 49.2% gross margin against a 42–45% five-year band, with oil back near $91 as of this week.
- **A large equity raise executed at what proved to be the top,** roughly 42% above today's price, into a balance sheet that was already in net cash and self-funding.
- **Return on equity permanently reset lower** by that raise, from roughly 35% toward roughly 26%, without a corresponding step-up in earnings power yet visible.
- **Capital spending at 8.5 times depreciation** into a decelerating top line.
- **Consensus is stranded 17% too high on 2026 revenue.** The estimate cuts have not happened yet.
- **This is sector-wide, not company-specific.** Mixue Group (2097.HK) is down from HK$499.60 to HK$223.40; Want Want (0151.HK) from HK$5.97 to HK$3.30; Nongfu Spring (9633.HK) from HK$56.25 to HK$42.16. The de-rating of Chinese branded beverages is a shared factor. Nothing about Eastroc's discount is idiosyncratic edge.

**🟢 Green flags**

- **The earnings are cash.** Operating cash flow at 1.49 times net profit, receivables under two days of sales, a negative cash conversion cycle, no goodwill anywhere on the balance sheet.
- **Real net cash.** RMB 23.21bn of cash and short-term investments against RMB 6.06bn of total debt including leases — RMB 17.15bn net, about 24% of the market value of the equity at the Hong Kong price.
- **Profit growth still outpacing revenue growth.** First-half 2026 earnings up 20.4% on revenue up 15.6%, with net margin up 90 basis points to 23.0%.
- **Free cash flow of RMB 4.86bn over the trailing year** — a yield of about 6.8% on the Hong Kong market value. Today's regime note explicitly says free cash flow, not revenue, is the current discriminator; this name screens well on exactly that test.
- **Buybacks started in the June quarter,** RMB 1.04bn of treasury stock created from nothing.
- **A genuine leading position** in a category where the brand, the price point and the reach into several million small independent retailers are hard to replicate quickly.

---

## 7. Hidden signals

- **The share count tells the story the press release would not.** 520.0m weighted-average shares in 2024; 676.0m in 2025 (a bonus issue, exactly 1.3 times); 734.1m issued by June 2026 after the Hong Kong listing. Anyone comparing 2026 earnings per share against 2024 earnings per share without adjusting for both events will reach the wrong conclusion. The reported 2025 figure of RMB 6.53 and the trailing figure of RMB 6.74 look almost flat — but the underlying profit went from RMB 4.42bn to RMB 4.90bn. The flatness is dilution, not stagnation.
- **The two listings disagree about what this company is worth.** The Shanghai A-shares closed at RMB 122.57; the Hong Kong H-shares at HK$114.60, which is RMB 98.34. The Hong Kong line trades at a 19.8% discount to the mainland line for identical economic ownership. That discount is a structural feature of dual-listed Chinese companies driven by capital controls and a different investor base, and it very rarely closes. Any valuation work that treats the gap as latent upside is double-counting.
- **The cheapest genuine comparison is not the cheap one.** On enterprise value to earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation — the standard way to compare operating businesses while ignoring differences in debt — Eastroc trades at about 9.3 times on the Hong Kong price. Nongfu Spring is at 17.6 times and Monster Beverage at 29.9 times, which makes Eastroc look very cheap. But Mixue Group, the Chinese beverage franchise that listed in Hong Kong in the same recent cohort and has fallen just as hard, trades at 8.3 times — *cheaper* than Eastroc. The discount is a cohort discount.
- **The buyback and the raise, six months apart, are the most eloquent thing in the file.** Management sold equity at roughly HK$197 and started buying it back below HK$150. That is a management team that reads its own valuation well. It is also a reminder that the shareholder on the other side of the first trade has lost 42%.

---

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict

**Classification: STABLE.**

This is not a deteriorating business. Revenue is still growing in the mid-teens, profit in the low twenties, margins are at records, the balance sheet is in substantial net cash, and the cash conversion is among the cleanest one encounters. What has deteriorated is the *rate* of growth and the *return on equity*, and one of those two is a direct consequence of a financing decision rather than of trading.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing.** The trailing multiple of about 14.6 times earnings, or roughly 12 times once the net cash is stripped out, is being computed on earnings that sit on a record 49.2% gross margin. If the input-cost tailwind reverses — and with crude back near $91 as of this week, the mechanism for that reversal is live right now — the "cheap" multiple is being paid on peak profits. That, not the growth deceleration, is the question that decides whether this is a mispriced franchise or a well-run company at a fair price.

**Economic moat.** The moat type is **intangible brand combined with scale in distribution**: a leading energy-drink brand plus reach into a very large base of small independent retailers, which is expensive and slow for a challenger to replicate. The evidence for it is strong on one axis and weak on another. Gross margin *expanding* from 44.8% to 48.1% is the cleanest possible evidence a moat is not eroding; a business losing pricing power does not do that. Against that, return on invested capital has fallen from 22.6% to 17.8%, revenue growth has halved, and the franchise is a single product category in a single country facing a well-capitalised incumbent and a crowded field in hydration drinks. That combination is **narrow but real**, and **stable** — not wide, because the position is concentrated and replicable given time and money; not eroding, because the margin evidence directly contradicts erosion and the return decline is largely the arithmetic consequence of a doubled equity base.

**Secular threat: manageable.** None of the structural forces that permanently impair terminal value — software and artificial intelligence displacing a service, payment networks being disintermediated, audiences abandoning a distribution channel, reimbursement being compressed — has any purchase on a company that sells caffeinated drinks in bottles to Chinese convenience stores. The channel through which those drinks reach consumers is shifting (instant delivery, e-commerce), which is a real operating challenge, but it is not a terminal-value question. The risks here are cyclical and competitive: Chinese consumer demand, input costs, and whether the second product line scales. The cheapness is therefore **not** a melting-ice-cube discount. Whether it is a mispricing or simply a fair price for a decelerating grower depends entirely on the margin question above.

Management credibility 3 of 5 · trajectory steady · a narrow but real moat · moat trend steady · structural threat manageable.

bull_thesis:
Eastroc Beverage, better known in China as Dongpeng, is the country's fastest-growing energy-drink brand, and the case for owning the Hong Kong-listed shares at HKD 104.60 is that the market has re-priced a genuinely excellent business as though its growth had stopped, when in fact it merely normalised.

Start with what is not in dispute. Over the trailing twelve months to 30 June 2026 the company earned CNY 4.90bn of net profit on CNY 22.55bn of revenue, a 21.7% net margin, and converted almost all of it into cash (free cash flow of CNY 4.86bn). Return on equity is 33.7%, and that is after February's Hong Kong listing added roughly CNY 9.7bn of fresh equity that is still sitting in bank deposits doing very little. The balance sheet at 30 June 2026 holds CNY 14.47bn of cash plus CNY 8.74bn of short-term investments against CNY 6.06bn of total debt, giving net cash of CNY 17.15bn — on the settled count of 727,076,759 shares that is about a quarter of the traded market value. There is no refinancing risk, no covenant, no maturity wall.

Now the part the tape is ignoring. Growth halved in the first half of 2026 — revenue rose 15.6% to CNY 12.415bn, against 31.8% for the whole of 2025 — but profit rose faster than revenue, up 20.4% to CNY 2.860bn, and gross margin expanded from 45.7% to 49.2% in the June quarter. A company whose demand was genuinely breaking does not widen its margins while it slows. What actually happened is that a 35%-a-year compounder became a mid-teens compounder with better unit economics, which is the normal life cycle of a successful consumer brand, not a warning.

The moat shows up in the working capital rather than in any slogan. Distributors pay Eastroc before they take delivery: customer prepayments stood at CNY 5.13bn at 30 June 2026, equal to 23% of a year's revenue. Receivables turn in under ten days, payables run 53 days, and the cash conversion cycle — the time between paying for goods and being paid for them — is minus 20.6 days. The company's own customers fund its growth. Very few businesses in any market are paid in advance by their channel; the ones that are tend to be the durable franchises.

Management is acting like the stock is cheap. Treasury stock of CNY 1.04bn appears on the 30 June 2026 balance sheet that was not there on 31 March — roughly a billion yuan of shares bought back during the quarter in which the shares fell hardest. The programme was executed at an average of CNY 145.84 an A share, well above today's CNY 121.98, so it is a statement about the company's own value range rather than a mark on today's price; it is still real capital committed rather than a press release.

Finally, the Hong Kong line is the cheap way in. At today's exchange rate of CNY 0.8559 to the Hong Kong dollar, the Hong Kong buyer pays CNY 89.53 per share for earnings the Shanghai buyer pays CNY 121.98 for — a 26.6% discount for identical economics. On the settled 727.1m share count the Hong Kong shares trade on about 13.3 times trailing earnings, 8.1 times enterprise value to earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, and 9.9 times enterprise value to free cash flow. Nongfu Spring, the closest listed comparison for quality, trades today at roughly 24 times earnings and 15.7 times that same cash-profit measure on materially worse cash conversion.

For this to work, three things must hold. Revenue growth has to stabilise around the mid-teens rather than keep sliding — the 26 October 2026 third-quarter report is the first test. Gross margin has to hold above roughly 46% despite rising oil-linked bottle-resin costs. And the second-act products, chiefly the electrolyte drink, have to keep scaling against much larger entrants. If they do, a business earning 34% on equity with a quarter of its value in cash is worth meaningfully more than 13 times earnings.
bear_thesis:
The bear case is not that Eastroc is a bad business. It is that the recent earnings are flattered by something outside management's control, that the numbers the market is anchored to have not yet been cut, and that the only visible corporate bid was struck well above today's price.

Begin with the cheapness, because a large part of the advertised discount evaporates on inspection. Our own screening record shows a fair value of 392.98 and a 281% margin of safety. That figure extrapolates a 33%-a-year earnings growth rate that ended six months ago and, worse, compares a yuan-denominated output to a Hong Kong dollar price when the two currencies are 17% apart. It is arithmetically meaningless and must be discarded. The same record's 'earnings per share up only 2.0%' is the mirror-image error in the other direction — an artefact of the 3-for-10 bonus issue that took the share count from 520.0m to 676.0m, not an earnings stall. Once both errors are cleared and the denominator is settled at 727,076,759 shares, the stock trades on roughly 13 times trailing earnings and 3.3 times book value. That is a fair multiple for a mid-teens grower, not a distressed one — the bear case does not need the shares to be expensive, only to be priced for margins and volumes that may not arrive. Our own valuation stack agrees it is split: of five independent methods, two say the shares are overvalued (the earnings-power method by 84%, the owner-earnings method by 22%).

Second, the profit growth is being carried by a commodity windfall. Gross margin reached 49.2% in the June 2026 quarter against 45.7% a year earlier, a level the company has never sustained and which our screen flags as 1.35 standard deviations above the historical peak. Bottle resin is an oil derivative, and Brent crude rose 9.3% in the week to 4 September 2026 (USD 88.10 to USD 96.28) with the Strait of Hormuz shut. Strip the margin back to the 2025 level of 44.8% and roughly CNY 800m of annualised gross profit disappears — enough to turn 20% profit growth into low single digits on unchanged volumes. The one thing holding the earnings line up has just been handed a headwind.

Third, the published estimates are stale and have to come down. The consensus for the 2026 financial year, from 17 analysts, is revenue of CNY 28.09bn. The company delivered CNY 12.415bn in the first half. Getting to CNY 28.09bn requires roughly 55% second-half growth in a business that just printed 15.6%. Nobody would forecast that having seen the interim numbers, which means the estimates simply have not been revised. When they are, the stock will look more expensive on forward earnings than it does today, and downgrade cycles in Chinese consumer names have a way of running longer than the fundamentals warrant.

Fourth, the fall is a de-rating, not a dislocation. The shares came to Hong Kong in February 2026, ran to HKD 227.69, and have given it all back plus more. The Shanghai line fell almost as far, from CNY 241.06 to CNY 121.98, and Mixue — the other hot Chinese consumer listing of the same window — is down from HKD 465.80 to HKD 206.20. This is an entire cohort unwinding an initial-public-offering bubble. Buying the sixth month of a cohort de-rating on the grounds that the chart looks washed out has no edge in it, and a stock 2% off its 52-week low with no dated event to force a re-rate can spend a long time going nowhere.

Fifth, the one corporate bid in the file is not a valuation signal. The CNY 1.04bn repurchase that the bull case reads as management calling its own stock cheap was 7,122,551 A shares for CNY 1,038,719,867.57, an average of CNY 145.84, per the 2 September 2026 buyback progress announcement. That is roughly 20% above the CNY 121.98 the A shares fetch today. The company was buying, but it was buying higher; the programme says nothing about today's price being management's value point, and capital already spent above the current mark is not support beneath the shares.

What would confirm the bear case: third-quarter revenue growth on 26 October 2026 below roughly 12%, a gross margin back under 46%, or a fall in customer prepayments (CNY 5.13bn at 30 June) against the prior year, which would say distributors are destocking. consensus_delta:
The usual question for a beaten-down value name is whether the market is pricing terminal decline into a business with stable earnings power. Here the answer is more interesting, and it cuts against us as much as for us: **the price has already worked out what the published estimates have not.**

The specific street assumption that is factually wrong is the 2026 revenue consensus. Seventeen analysts carry an average of CNY 28.09bn in a strikingly tight band of CNY 27.74bn to CNY 28.50bn. Eastroc delivered CNY 12.44bn of revenue in the first half of 2026. Reaching the consensus therefore requires second-half revenue of CNY 15.65bn against CNY 10.13bn a year earlier — growth of 54% — from a company that just grew 15.9%. No analyst who had read the interim report would publish that number. The estimates have simply not been refreshed since the results, and our own screening record's 'consensus forward earnings growth +12.4%' inherits the same stale base. The consensus earnings figure of CNY 5.64bn is less absurd but still demands 36% second-half profit growth against 20.7% delivered in the first half.

So where we disagree with the market is not that we are more bullish than the street — we are more bearish than the printed numbers, and roughly level with the price. The stock at HKD 104.60 already reflects a mid-teens grower; the estimates still describe a 35% grower. When those estimates are cut, the headlines will read as a downgrade cycle even though the price has known for months. That is the trap in this name: the obvious contrarian read — 'everyone hates it, the numbers are fine' — has the causality backwards.

There is one place where we genuinely differ from the tape, and it is narrower than the drawdown suggests. The market is treating the deceleration as a quality event. It is not. Profit grew faster than revenue (+20.7% against +15.9%), gross margin widened from 45.7% to 49.2% in the June quarter, return on equity is 33.7% after a large dilutive equity raise, distributors still pay in advance to the tune of CNY 5.13bn, and the cash conversion cycle is minus 20.6 days. Those are not the fingerprints of a franchise losing grip. A business with those characteristics growing profit at 20% is worth more than 16 times earnings — but 'more' here means roughly 19 times, not the 40-plus times the shares carried in the spring. The mispricing is real and it is about 17% wide. It is not the 281% our own screen advertised, and the gap between those two numbers is the whole reason this record exists.
forcing_function:
There is no hard date, no proxy window and no corporate event that contractually forces a re-rating here, and it would be dishonest to manufacture one. What exists is a sequence of scheduled checkpoints at which the market can change its mind.

**26 October 2026 — the third-quarter report** (date listed on TradingView's company page, retrieved 7 September 2026). This is the moment that matters most in the next six months. It answers the only question that decides this name: did revenue growth stabilise in the mid-teens, or did it keep sliding? And did gross margin hold above 46% as bottle-resin costs began to rise? A print showing 15%-plus revenue growth with the margin intact converts this from a watchlist name into a buy, because it would confirm that a 34%-return, net-cash franchise is being valued as a cyclical. A print below 12% growth, or a margin under 46%, and the earnings base itself is in question rather than just the multiple.

**The customer prepayment line in that same report.** Contract liabilities were CNY 5.13bn at 30 June 2026. Set against the prior-year figure — which we could not obtain and which anyone underwriting this should insist on — it is the single best forward indicator in the accounts, because distributors pre-order before shipments show up in revenue.

**A continued or enlarged buyback.** The CNY 1.04bn repurchased in the June quarter is the company's own statement about value. Extending it materially at these prices would be the clearest signal management believes the fall has overshot.

**Estimate resets.** The published 2026 consensus needs to fall roughly 15% to become arithmetically possible. Paradoxically, that cut landing is a positive event, not a negative one: it removes the last reason for a marginal buyer to stay away, and it is the point at which the forward multiple stops being a fiction.
valley_of_death:
There is no cash-burn hump and no maturity wall here — with CNY 17.15bn of net cash, interest cover above 80 times and CNY 4.86bn of annual free cash flow, the company cannot be forced into anything. The risky window over the next three to nine months is entirely about earnings quality and the estimate cycle.

**The margin unwind is the live danger, and its clock has already started.** The June 2026 quarter's 49.2% gross margin is the highest the company has ever posted and our own screen flags it as 1.35 standard deviations above the historical peak. The most plausible driver is falling input costs — polyethylene terephthalate resin for the bottles and sugar. Brent crude rose 9.3% in the week to 4 September 2026, from USD 88.10 to USD 96.28, on resumed strikes with the Strait of Hormuz shut 189 days. Resin prices follow crude with a lag of roughly one to two quarters, which puts the cost increase into the December 2026 and March 2027 reporting periods. Reverting the margin to 2025's 44.8% removes roughly CNY 800m of annualised gross profit — enough to take profit growth from 20% to low single digits on unchanged volumes. This is the one place where the current market regime has a genuinely live transmission channel into this name, and it points the wrong way.

**The estimate cut is close to certain and has not happened yet.** Analysts are still carrying 54% second-half revenue growth. Those numbers will be marked down, most likely around the third-quarter report on 26 October 2026. Headline downgrade risk is therefore concentrated in the next seven weeks, and downgrade cycles in Chinese consumer names typically run in three or four waves rather than one.

**The cohort de-rating may not be finished.** Mixue is down 56% from its high, Nongfu is down 26%, and both Eastroc listings are down roughly half. Nothing in the tape says the unwind of the 2025-26 Chinese consumer listing boom has found its floor, and a stock sitting 2% off its 52-week low has no technical support beneath it.

**The measurement risk we cannot resolve.** The 22% discrepancy between the exchange's reported share count of 895.5m and the company's balance-sheet implied 734m is not itself a business risk, but it means any position taken today is sized against a denominator we have not verified. That is a reason to wait for clarity rather than to buy through it.
positioning_washout:
This is not a yield-driven shareholder base and there is no dividend cut in prospect, so the classic mechanical-liquidation setup does not apply. The dividend is roughly 2.1% of the price on the trailing payout of CNY 1.88 a share; note that two widely used data providers quote 5.5% and 6.0% for this name, both of which appear to annualise an older, higher payout against the new, much lower price. The forced-selling pressure that matters is the unwinding of an initial-public-offering shareholder register. The Hong Kong shares listed on 3 February 2026, ran to HKD 227.69, and are now at HKD 104.60 — roughly 45% below where the offering priced. Every investor who bought the deal or bought into the first-quarter enthusiasm is deeply underwater, and the standard six-month lock-up on such an offering would have expired around early August 2026. Working the other way, the company itself has been a buyer: roughly CNY 1.04bn of stock repurchased during the June 2026 quarter. That is the only large, price-insensitive bid visible in the file, and it is a real one.

The honest read is that the washout is well advanced but probably not complete. The shares sit 2% above their 52-week low and 29% below their 200-day average, which is the profile of a market still finding sellers rather than one that has run out of them. A capitulation low, if it comes, would most likely be printed around the third-quarter report when the estimate cuts land.
moderator_conclusion:
**Buy it here.** The first pass called this a good business at a fair price and told the committee to wait for roughly HKD 90. That instruction rested on a denominator that has since been settled against the company's own filings, and with the correct one the same schedule produces a different answer.

The quality was never the argument. Eastroc earns a 33.7% return on equity, converts essentially all of its profit into cash, carries CNY 17.15bn of net cash — about a quarter of its market value on the settled count — and is paid in advance by its distributors to the tune of 23% of a year's revenue. Its cash conversion cycle is minus 20.6 days. Those are the marks of a genuine consumer franchise, and they are why the moat reads as narrow but real and stable rather than eroding: the margins are widening, not contracting, and no structural force this committee tracks threatens the terminal value of Chinese functional beverages.

The price is no longer the problem. On 727,076,759 shares outstanding the shares trade at about 13.3 times trailing earnings and 3.3 times book, roughly 10 times once net cash is stripped out. Base fair value is HKD 150 against a HKD 104.60 quote — a 30.3% discount, which clears this book's 20% entry-discount floor in the current GOLDILOCKS quadrant rather than missing it. Against an adverse case of HKD 82 the trade-off is 43% up for 22% down, a reward to risk of 2.01 where the first pass computed 0.46. There is still no structural floor: net cash is worth about HKD 27.5 a share and there is no deal, tender or fixed distribution to catch the price, so the downside remains bounded by the multiple.

Two of the three things that previously held the conviction at neutral survive; the third does not. The growth reset is real — 15.6% revenue growth in the first half of 2026 against 31.8% for 2025, confirmed on both listings — and the profit growth that survives is riding on a record 49.2% gross margin most plausibly caused by falling oil-linked input costs, with Brent up 9.3% in the week to 4 September 2026 and the Strait of Hormuz shut. That is the one place where the current regime reaches directly into this business, and it points against us; it is why the 18-month horizon and a mid-teens, not a mid-thirties, growth assumption are carried. The third holdback, the unresolved share count, is gone: 734,199,310 issued less 7,122,551 in treasury gives 727,076,759, tied to the interim distribution total and the Q2 weighted-average count. The record's own conservatism has been paid back rather than punished.

One bear-side fact travels with the correction and is worth stating plainly. The CNY 1.04bn buyback was executed at an average of CNY 145.84 an A share against CNY 121.98 today, so it is evidence of management's value range, not confirmation that today's price is their entry. It should not be read as a bid beneath the stock.

On the catalyst, we apply no penalty and no credit. The listing has happened and its re-rating has fully reversed; the buyback has happened; what remains is a soft catalyst with no fixed date and no contractual payout. In this book that is a description, not a mark against the name — but it is also why this is a conviction 4 and not higher: the discount is wide and the balance sheet is unarguable, yet nothing on the calendar forces the re-rating. The **26 October 2026 third-quarter report** remains the test that either accelerates it or breaks it: revenue growth holding at 15% or better with gross margin above 46% despite rising resin costs, and customer prepayments up year on year, and the case strengthens; a print below 12% growth or a margin under 46% and the earnings base, not just the multiple, is in question. Verdict held at B — the setup is a wide discount on a quality compounder without a dated forcing event, which is exactly what a B describes — with conviction lifted from 3 to 4 because the arithmetic that argued for waiting no longer does.
